stimuli.text: Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
A student heats 11.2 g of $$\ce{CaCO3(s)}$$, which decomposes completely: $$\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$$. The $$\ce{CO2}$$ is collected at 301 K and 1.02 atm.
The decomposition of compound X was monitored at constant temperature.
A student titrates 32.0 mL of 0.18 M weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka = 3 \times 10^{-5}) with 0.19 M NaOH.
3.8 g of $$\ce{NaOH}$$ dissolves in 67 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature rises by 6.2 °C. Assume the solution's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·°C).

A galvanic cell is made of a Zn electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Zn^{2+}}$$ and a Pb electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Pb^{2+}}$$. Standard reduction potentials: $$\ce{Zn^{2+} + 2e- -> Zn}$$ E° = -0.76 V; $$\ce{Pb^{2+} + 2e- -> Pb}$$ E° = -0.13 V.
The photoelectron spectra of Na (Z = 11) and Mg (Z = 12) are compared.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.01 M solution of $$\ce{HNO3}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: Correct. Strong acid: [H₃O⁺] equals its concentration.
Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 13.5 g. The actual yield is 10.7 g. What is the percent yield?
How many formula units or molecules are in 125 g of $$\ce{C6H12O6}$$?

options.why: Correct. Convert grams to moles, then multiply by Avogadro's number.

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{CO2}$$, $$\ce{Ar}$$, $$\ce{He}$$, $$\ce{N2}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: CO2 has a larger molar mass (44 g/mol).
N2 has a larger molar mass (28 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
Ar has a larger molar mass (40 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: CO2 44, Ar 40, He 4, N2 28.

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 30. What is K for the reaction multiplied by ½?

options.why: K is raised to a power, not multiplied.
Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.
Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.

questions.stem: Which bond is the most polar?

options.why: Correct. It has the largest electronegativity difference (1.2).

questions.stem: 55 g of water at 81 °C is mixed with 61 g of water at 14 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?

options.why: Pair each mass with its own temperature.
Correct. Heat lost = heat gained; for water alone, a mass-weighted average.

questions.stem: If ΔH = −286 kJ for H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O(l), what is ΔH for 2H₂O(l) → 2H₂ + O₂?
A solution has an absorbance of 1.38 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 692 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
A solution has an absorbance of 0.247 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 411 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
What is the hybridization of the central atom in $$\ce{H2O}$$?

options.why: Count electron domains, including lone pairs.
Correct. Hybridization matches the number of electron domains: 2 sp, 3 sp², 4 sp³.
Count electron domains, including lone pairs.
Count electron domains, including lone pairs.

questions.explanation: H2O has 4 electron domains on the central atom.

questions.stem: How many valence electrons are shown in the Lewis structure of $$\ce{SO2}$$?

options.why: Correct. Sum the valence electrons of all atoms, then add one per negative charge (subtract one per positive charge).

questions.stem: Which change alters the value of K?
Which process has a negative ΔS?
Samples of $$\ce{N2}$$, $$\ce{CO2}$$, $$\ce{CH4}$$, $$\ce{He}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
CH4 has a larger molar mass (16 g/mol).
N2 has a larger molar mass (28 g/mol).
CO2 has a larger molar mass (44 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: N2 28, CO2 44, CH4 16, He 4.

questions.stem: When a reaction involving 0.095 mol of limiting reactant occurs in 246 g of solution (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), the temperature falls by 8.9 °C. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Divide by the moles of reactant.
A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic (negative ΔH).
Correct. q(solution) = mcΔT = 9150 J; q(reaction) = −q(solution); divide by moles.

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{Ar}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$, $$\ce{Cl2}$$, $$\ce{CH4}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: CH4 has a larger molar mass (16 g/mol).
Ar has a larger molar mass (40 g/mol).
Cl2 has a larger molar mass (70.9 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.

questions.explanation: Molar masses: Ar 40, H2 2.02, Cl2 70.9, CH4 16.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.1 mol N₂, 0.7 mol O₂ and 0.9 mol Ar at a total pressure of 2.4 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.3 mol N₂, 0.5 mol O₂ and 0.9 mol Ar at a total pressure of 3.3 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{Cl2}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$, $$\ce{CH4}$$, $$\ce{N2}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: CH4 has a larger molar mass (16 g/mol).
Cl2 has a larger molar mass (70.9 g/mol).
N2 has a larger molar mass (28 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.

questions.explanation: Molar masses: Cl2 70.9, H2 2.02, CH4 16, N2 28.

questions.stem: 24 mL of 6 M solution is diluted to 386 mL. What is the new concentration?

options.why: V₂ is the total final volume.

questions.stem: A 28.1 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 22.6 mL of 0.251 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 40 kJ/mol, the transition state at 148 kJ/mol and the products at 158 kJ/mol. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Measure from the correct starting point.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 108, ΔH = 118, reverse Ea = -10 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 321 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$ is consumed at 0.37 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{NH3}$$ form?

options.why: Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.
Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 2/3.

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 9 min. Starting at 17.9 M, what is the concentration after 36 min?

options.why: Each half-life halves the concentration; it is not divided by 2n.

questions.stem: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, $$\ce{CaO}$$ or $$\ce{MgF2}$$?

options.text: $$\ce{MgF2}$$, because its ions have larger charges
They are equal because both are ionic
$$\ce{CaO}$$, because its ions have larger charges
options.why: Correct. By Coulomb's law, attraction increases with the product of the ion charges.

options.text: $$\ce{MgF2}$$, because it has more atoms per formula unit
options.why: Number of atoms does not determine lattice energy.

questions.explanation: CaO has ion charges 2 and 2; MgF2 has 2 and 1.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of O in $$\ce{H2O2}$$?

options.why: Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Correct. The oxidation numbers must sum to the species' overall charge (O usually −2, H usually +1).
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.

questions.stem: How should acetic acid be written in a net ionic equation?

options.why: Correct. It is a weak acid and mostly un-ionized.

options.text: It is always omitted as a spectator

questions.explanation: It is a weak acid and mostly un-ionized.

questions.stem: Which formula is most likely for the compound of element X (Group 2) and element Y (Group 16)?
Adding an inert gas to a reaction mixture at constant volume does what to the equilibrium?

options.text: Shifts it toward fewer gas moles
Shifts it toward more gas moles
Nothing; partial pressures of the reacting gases are unchanged

questions.stem: 35 mL of 0.16 M weak acid HA is titrated with 0.21 M NaOH. What volume of NaOH reaches the equivalence point?

options.why: Correct. Moles of base = moles of acid.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$ is consumed at 0.49 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{NH3}$$ form?

options.why: Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.
Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 2/3.

questions.stem: A 20.4 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 45 mL of 0.183 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: What is the mass percent of C in $$\ce{C3H8}$$?

options.why: That is the percent of the other elements.
There are 3 atoms of C in the formula.
Use masses, not numbers of atoms.

questions.stem: Steel is harder than pure iron because:

options.text: Carbon replaces iron atoms of the same size
Small carbon atoms in the gaps (interstitial alloy) hinder layers of iron atoms from sliding

questions.stem: Why does I₂ have a higher boiling point than Br₂?

options.text: I₂ has a larger, more polarizable electron cloud, so stronger London dispersion forces
options.why: Correct. Dispersion forces grow with polarizability.
Boiling does not break covalent bonds.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 3.4. In a solution at pH 1.5, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Below the pKa, the protonated form dominates.

questions.stem: How many moles of gas are in a 25 L flask at 3.02 atm and 404 K?
A weak acid (pKa 6.35) is titrated with NaOH; the equivalence point is reached at 17.4 mL. What is the pH after 8.68 mL of NaOH has been added?

options.why: That is only for strong acid–strong base equivalence.
Correct. At the half-equivalence point, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.

questions.stem: At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is -10 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = 4.04; K = 56.6. Negative ΔG°: K greater than 1.

questions.stem: For a reaction, ΔH° = 161 kJ/mol and ΔS° = -75 J/(mol·K). What is ΔG° at 650 K, and is the reaction favorable?

options.why: Correct. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, with ΔS in kJ/(mol·K).
Convert ΔS from J to kJ.

questions.stem: For the elementary step 2NO + Cl₂ → 2NOCl, what is the rate law?

options.text: It cannot be determined without experiment

options.why: Correct. Elementary steps use their coefficients as exponents.

questions.explanation: Elementary steps use their coefficients as exponents.

questions.stem: Which indicator is best for titrating acetic acid with NaOH (equivalence pH ≈ 8.7)?

options.why: Correct. Its range includes the equivalence pH.

questions.explanation: Its range includes the equivalence pH.

questions.stem: A compound (tetraphosphorus decoxide) is 43.6% P, 56.4% O by mass. What is its empirical formula?

options.why: That is the molecular formula; reduce to the simplest ratio.
Correct. Convert each percent (in 100 g) to moles and divide by the smallest.

questions.explanation: The mole ratio reduces to P2O5; the molecular formula is P4O10.

questions.stem: For a reaction, ΔH° = -110 kJ/mol and ΔS° = 235 J/(mol·K). What is ΔG° at 606 K, and is the reaction favorable?

options.why: Correct. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, with ΔS in kJ/(mol·K).
Convert ΔS from J to kJ.

questions.stem: 48 mL of 0.19 M weak acid HA is titrated with 0.15 M NaOH. What volume of NaOH reaches the equivalence point?

options.why: Correct. Moles of base = moles of acid.

questions.stem: A photoelectron spectrum shows 6 peaks. From highest to lowest binding energy, their relative heights are 2 : 2 : 6 : 2 : 6 : 1. Which element is it?

options.why: Correct. The peaks correspond to $$1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{6}\,3s^{2}\,3p^{6}\,4s^{1}$$, which has 19 electrons.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O}$$, 55 g of $$\ce{C3H8}$$ reacts with 75 g of $$\ce{O2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{CO2}$$ can form?

options.why: Not all of both reactants reacts.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.
Apply the mole ratio from the equation.
Correct. O2 is the limiting reactant.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 1 M solution of nitrous acid (Ka = 4.5 \times 10^{-4})?

options.why: A weak acid does not ionize completely.
Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].

questions.stem: For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 9.1. A mixture has [A] = 0.5 M, [B] = 0.4 M and [C] = 0.8 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 3.2
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 3.2, which is less than K.

options.text: It is at equilibrium, because Q = K
It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 4
It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 3.2
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

questions.stem: What is E°cell for a galvanic cell made from these half-cells?

options.why: Cathode minus anode; a galvanic cell is positive.
E° does not change when half-reactions are multiplied.

questions.stem: A mass spectrum of a sample of copper shows two peaks: mass 63 with relative abundance 61% and mass 65 with 39%. What is the average atomic mass of the sample?

options.why: Pair each mass with its own abundance.
The isotopes are not equally abundant.
Correct. Weight each isotope mass by its fractional abundance.

questions.stem: What is the rate law?

options.why: Compare trials where only one concentration changes.
Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.
Recheck how the rate changes when [B] doubles.
Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 1; doubling [B] multiplies it by 2.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×1, so order 0 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×2, so order 1 in B.

questions.stem: The Ksp of $$\ce{Mg(OH)2}$$ is 5.6 \times 10^{-12}. What is its molar solubility in pure water?
Use the bond enthalpies to estimate ΔH for $$\ce{H2 + F2 -> 2HF}$$.

options.why: Bonds formed release energy: subtract them.
Correct. ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
Multiply each bond energy by the number of bonds.
Broken minus formed, not formed minus broken.

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.25 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 7.21) and 0.34 mol of its conjugate base A⁻. Then 0.03 mol of HCl is added. What is the pH?

options.why: Correct. First react: H⁺ converts A⁻ to HA. Then pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).
Update moles after the added acid or base reacts.

questions.stem: Reaction 1 has ΔH₁ = -239 kJ and reaction 2 has ΔH₂ = 170 kJ. A target reaction is obtained by doubling reaction 1 and reversing reaction 2. What is ΔH for the target reaction?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → change sign; multiply → multiply ΔH; then add.
Reversing changes the sign of ΔH₂.
Enthalpies add; they do not multiply.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$$, initial [H₂] = 0.5 M and [I₂] = 1.9 M, with no HI. At equilibrium, [HI] = 0.36 M. What is K?
Calculate ΔH° for $$\ce{C2H5OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 3H2O(l)}$$. (ΔH°f of O₂ is 0.)

options.why: Multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient.
Correct. Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants).

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ produced.

rubric.criterion: Correct moles using molar mass 100.09 g/mol and the 1:1 ratio.

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of CO₂ expected.
The student measures 2.195 L of gas. Calculate the percent yield, and give one experimental reason the yield could be less than 100%.

rubric.example: Incomplete decomposition (not heated long enough) or gas leaking from the apparatus.

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a complete Lewis diagram for CO₂, and identify its molecular geometry and the hybridization of carbon.

rubric.example: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O (16 valence electrons).

parts.prompt: Explain why CO₂ is nonpolar even though C=O bonds are polar.

rubric.criterion: Linear symmetry makes the bond dipoles cancel.

parts.prompt: CaO is an ionic solid. Explain, using Coulomb's law, why CaO has a higher melting point than KCl.

rubric.criterion: Larger ion charges in CaO (2+/2−) than in KCl (1+/1−).
Greater electrostatic attraction (and smaller ions) means more energy is needed to separate the ions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of disappearance of X between 0 and 20 s.
Determine the order of the reaction with respect to X. Justify your answer using the data.

rubric.example: Equal time intervals give equal changes in 1/[X].

parts.prompt: Write the rate law and determine the rate constant, with units.
Calculate the half-life of the reaction (for the initial concentration).
A proposed mechanism has a slow first step: 2X → X₂. Is the mechanism consistent with the rate law? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Yes; the slow step's elementary rate law matches the observed rate law.

parts.prompt: A catalyst is added. Explain its effect on the rate and on the rate constant, using activation energy.

rubric.example: The catalyst provides a new pathway.

rubric.criterion: Lower activation energy means a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

parts.prompt: Write the net ionic equation for the titration reaction.
Calculate the initial pH of the acid solution.

rubric.criterion: Ka expression set up with x = [H₃O⁺].

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point.
What is the pH at the half-equivalence point? Justify.
Calculate the pH at the equivalence point.

rubric.criterion: Uses Kb = Kw/Ka and the diluted [A⁻].

parts.prompt: Choose an appropriate indicator from: methyl orange (pKa 3.7), bromothymol blue (pKa 7.0), phenolphthalein (pKa 9.3). Justify.

rubric.criterion: Indicator whose pKa is closest to the equivalence pH.

parts.prompt: Explain why the solution at the half-equivalence point resists pH change when a small amount of HCl is added.

rubric.criterion: A⁻ reacts with added H⁺ to form HA (buffer).
rubric.example: A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA + H₂O, so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes only slightly.

parts.prompt: Is the dissolution endothermic or exothermic? Justify.

rubric.example: Exothermic: the solution warmed, so energy was released.

parts.prompt: Calculate the heat absorbed or released by the solution.
Calculate ΔH of dissolution in kJ/mol.
If some heat escaped to the surroundings, would the magnitude of the calculated ΔH be too large or too small? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Too small, because the measured temperature change is smaller than the true change.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the cell reaction.
Calculate E°cell.
Calculate ΔG° for the cell reaction.
The concentration of Zn²⁺ is increased to 2.0 M. Predict the effect on the cell potential and justify.

rubric.criterion: E decreases because Q increases (a product's concentration rises).
rubric.example: Q greater than 1 → E less than E°.

questions.title: Solubility of a slightly soluble salt

parts.prompt: Write the Ksp expression.
Calculate the molar solubility in pure water.
Calculate the molar solubility in a solution containing 0.1 M I⁻ (from a soluble salt).
Would lowering the pH significantly change the solubility? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Correct reasoning about whether the anion is basic.
rubric.example: No: I⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid, so H⁺ does not remove it.

parts.prompt: Write the electron configuration of Mg.
Explain why the 1s peak of Mg has a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of Na.

rubric.criterion: Mg has more protons, so 1s electrons are attracted more strongly (Coulomb's law).

parts.prompt: Describe one difference in the number or relative height of peaks between the two spectra.

rubric.criterion: A valid difference based on configurations.
rubric.example: Mg has one more electron, so its outermost peak is taller or an extra peak appears.

parts.prompt: Which element has the larger atomic radius? Justify using Coulomb's law.

rubric.criterion: Na: fewer protons with similar shielding, so valence electrons are held less tightly.
rubric.example: Same period; effective nuclear charge increases across.
